Maladaptive Strategies.value: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Fire/flame cues are hard to reconcile with a childhood domestic-violence witnessing trauma profile when the rest of the trigger, memory, threat, and appraisal items do not suggest fire, arson, or burn-related trauma content. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
issues.explanation: 'No longer capable of doing the things that defined me' suggests a loss of prior adult identity/functioning that is difficult to fit with a 19-year-old whose index trauma was childhood witnessed domestic violence. The other appraisals center on helplessness and failed protection, which fit better; this item is comparatively implausible for the developmental context.

vignette: As a child, Maria had grown accustomed to the sound of her father's anger. It was a low hum in the background of their lives, always simmering just below the surface. But one night, it boiled over into something more sinister. She remembered the darkness of the room, the feeling of being small and helpless as she watched her mother cower under her father's rage. The sounds still echoed in her mind - the shouting, the crashing, the sickening thud of flesh hitting flesh. Years later, Maria found herself working as a train conductor, responsible for ensuring the safety of hundreds of passengers every day. But despite her outward confidence and competence, she couldn't shake off the feeling of vulnerability that lingered long after her childhood trauma. She worked tirelessly to keep busy, filling every spare moment with tasks and responsibilities, trying to outrun the memories that haunted her. At night, as the train rumbled through dark tunnels or pulled into deserted stations, Maria's heart would begin to pound in her chest. The darkness seemed to close in around her, making it hard to breathe. She would try to distract herself by checking and rechecking the doors and windows of the train cars, ensuring that everything was secure, but even those familiar rituals couldn't calm her racing thoughts. Loud noises still made her jump - the screech of brakes, the blast of a horn, or the sudden rumble of thunder. Her body would tense up, ready to defend itself against an invisible threat. And when she heard these sounds, Maria's mind would transport her back to that fateful night, reliving the terror and helplessness all over again. The memories themselves were fragmented and disjointed, like a puzzle with missing pieces. Maria couldn't quite put them in order - what had happened before, during, or after the violence? But one thing she remembered clearly was the taste of her mother's cooking that night, a savory smell that still made her stomach turn whenever it wafted back into her consciousness. Maria often wondered how her life would have been different if that event had never occurred. Would she be more confident, less fearful? She replayed scenarios in her head, imagining alternative outcomes where she was brave enough to intervene, or where her father's anger was somehow contained. But those thoughts only led to more guilt and self-blame - why hadn't she done something to stop it? As a result, Maria struggled with feelings of helplessness, convinced that bad things would always happen no matter what she did. She felt like a failure for not protecting her mother, for not being able to prevent the trauma from unfolding. Her only coping mechanism was to restrict her food intake, eating as little as possible in an attempt to maintain some semblance of control over her life. Despite her busy schedule and attempts at distraction, Maria couldn't shake off the feeling that danger lurked around every corner. She found herself constantly on high alert, even when she knew rationally that there was no immediate threat. It was exhausting, living like this - perpetually waiting for the other shoe to drop, never quite able to exhale. It was only when Maria started missing shifts due to anxiety and sleeplessness that she realized she needed help. Her loved ones had been encouraging her to seek therapy for months, but it wasn't until she hit rock bottom that she finally acknowledged the toll her trauma was taking on her life. As she sat in her therapist's office, fidgeting with her hands, Maria knew that she wanted to learn how to quiet the cacophony of sounds and emotions inside her head. She hoped to find a way to break free from the darkness that had haunted her for so long, and finally start living in the present rather than being forever trapped in the past.
